title: How Netflix Evaluates AI When There's No Right Answer - Cameron Wolfe, Netflix

segments.text: All right, well, hi everybody. I'm
Cameron Wolfe. I'm a staff research
scientist at Netflix. I also write the
deep learning focused newsletter.
Hopefully you read it. And today I'm
going to be talking about evaluations
and more specifically trying to evaluate
highly subjective tasks.
And we're going to go over a lot of
information.
Uh
it's supposed to be kind of like an
overview. If there's anything that you
want to look into in more depth, you
could scan this QR code. It'll take you
to the slides. I've also written a lot
of stuff that outlines all of these
different concepts in detail. So
plenty opportunity for further reading
if there's anything that you're
interested in throughout the talk.
So, we all know evaluations are
difficult. We've seen a lot of
presentations on this during AIEE. And
if we think about why this is the case,
there's just there's evidence of this
everywhere within the AI research
community. People are talking about
benchmarking constantly. There's new
evals being released like every day in
different revisions the evals. So, we
all know that evaluations are difficult.
But if we step back and think about why
this is the case, there are a couple of
different reasons. And one of the
primary reasons and the one that we're
going to focus on a lot today is noise.
We're working with several
non-deterministic components when we're
trying to evaluate models. This creates
a lot of fluctuations in behavior and it
just makes it really difficult to draw
reliable conclusions from eval results.
And to understand why this is the case,
we can just look at the structure of an
evaluation trial. So, we have our
evaluation suite here. It's composed of
a bunch of different tasks that we want
to try and solve. We pass these of those
tasks to a non-deterministic agent that
gives us a rollout and eventually a
solution. And then we take this solution
and pass it to a grader which will give
us just some some kind of pass fail
result. So, at the end of the day we're
just trying to get our agents to solve
these tasks and seeing if they're
passing them or not.
And because of the cost of evaluation,
you know, some of these recent
benchmarks will cost like, you know, 50,
100,000 dollars to run them. Uh we can't
evaluate over that many tasks. So, the
set of tasks within our evaluation
benchmark typically is going to be
relatively small. And this combined with
the fact that we're already working with
a non-deterministic agent, it already
just makes it difficult to have any sort
of like reliance on the eval result.
And on top of this, if we look at most
of the stuff that people are working on
in terms of evals, we're primarily
focusing on verifiable tasks. So, this
grader that we see at the bottom of the
screen here, it's implemented as some
sort of like deterministic check,
whether it be string matching, symbolic
verification, test cases, and so on.
Uh so, we're mostly focusing on these
verifiable tasks where pass-fail is
something that we can evaluate with a
function.
But if we look at the different things
that an agent will try and do in the
real world, it kind of lies on a
spectrum of verifiability. Not all tasks
are verifiable.
So, on one end of the spectrum, we have
things like math where we can verify
solutions deterministically with things
like string matching or symbolic
verification.
But on the other end of the spectrum, we
have super subjective tasks like
creative writing. And here, the
definition of pass-fail is extremely
subjective and open-ended, and it's hard
even for humans to evaluate reliably.
So, usually we're going to have to draw
upon some type of like LM judge or
rubric to help us with this.
And what we end up with is that we're
taking a component that was previously
deterministic, this grader, and we're
replacing it with another
non-deterministic LM-based component.
So, we just end up with a lot of noise
and subjectivity within an evaluation
process that was already difficult to
begin with. Um so, what we end up with
with this is just something that looks
like this. We're drowning in all this
noise. Uh we're completely blind to if
our agent is like doing well or not. So,
the goal of the talk today is to try and
figure out how to not become this
person.
So, what we're going to do is we're
going to outline a repeatable three-part
framework for evaluating super
subjective tasks. This will consist of
offline evaluation, human evaluation,
and production monitoring. And then
we're going to outline the best
practices for each of these components,
which applies both to subjective tasks
and just to evaluation in general.
And then along the way we're going to
cover a bunch of different tricks that
we can use to reduce noise, have more
statistical like confidence in these
evaluation results, and just dry the
most dry dry the most reliable
conclusions that we can from our
evaluation results.
So, let's get into it.
So, when we're working on a very
subjective or open-ended task, the first
step is to set up a human evaluation
process. And this is going to be the
North Star for defining, measuring, and
improving the quality of our task over
time.
But, in order to set up human
evaluation, we need to first create a
clear definition of what quality means.
And usually the way that we do this is
by partnering with some small number of
subject matter experts to create quality
guidelines.
And within these quality guidelines for
our task, we define a small set of
criteria that we care about in terms of
what should be in the final solution. We
define how to rate these criteria,
usually using some type of like binary
or Likert score. And then we just
provide a ton of details defining what
each of these criteria are, specific
examples of how to rate them, and things
like this. So, we want to provide humans
as much information possible so that we
can minimize the subjectivity of this
human evaluation process.
But, even if we write the best possible
human evaluation guidelines, we can't
just assume that the human evaluation
process is going to be reliable. So, we
need to calibrate it extensively. And
what this means concretely is that we
take multiple human evaluation samples
for the same data, look at the agreement
between them, and then update our
guidelines based upon the sources of
disagreement that we see. So, this is
kind of an iterative process where
you're literally just talking with
humans and trying to see, you know, is
there some issue in my guideline that
makes it unclear how to evaluate this?
And over time, we want to make our
quality guidelines as clear as possible
so we can get high agreement between all
of these different humans.
So, if we do this properly, then we end
up with a calibrated human evaluation
process and very clear quality
guidelines. And we can already use this
to start performing evaluations. But, if
we want to draw some sort of reliable
conclusion from these human evaluations,
we also need to think about how we
sample data.
So, we need to think about things like
the amount of data that we're going to
put into the evaluation process, the
type of data that we will evaluate on
and so forth.
And for the amount of data, we can draw
upon a statistical concept called power
analysis, which will help us understand
the amount of data that we need to pass
into the evaluation process.
And power is a really interesting area
of statistics, but for the purposes of
this presentation, the high-level idea
is that power analysis allows us to
estimate the volume of data that we need
to put into the evaluation process to
make a meaningful conclusion about the
difference in performance between two
different models.
And we make this estimation by looking
at things like the effect size that we
want to detect, the level of noise that
we observe in our eval results. You can
estimate this with like resampling model
completions and so forth, and the
desired significance level. So, how
confident we want to be that a
difference in two models' performance is
actually legitimate and not due to
noise. So, we can use power analysis
with these factors to estimate the size
of our eval that we need for a reliable
conclusion.
And then in terms of the type of data
that we want to sample, there are a
bunch of different factors, but at a
high level, if you read a bunch of
different benchmark reports and see what
people do, generally they're going to
focus upon diversity and the realism of
the evaluation. So, we want all of the
data that we evaluate on to accurately
reflect the types of tasks that the
agent is solving in production. We want
it to be difficult and discriminative,
meaning that it differentiates between
the capabilities of different models.
Usually, this is assessed via some form
of like profiling, just sampling
rollouts and seeing what types of
problems a model can actually solve
versus not. And then we want it to be as
accurate as possible, which is usually
accomplished via some combination of
like model and human-based filtering
over time.
And these concepts for sampling data
properly, they're not only applicable to
human evaluation. You can kind of use
these anywhere. So, we'll also see again
in the future when we talk about offline
evals, we'll probably use like very
similar data sampling techniques.
So, at this point, we have a reliable
human evaluation process, but the
problem is if we want to human evaluate
every new agent or model that we're
looking into, uh it's quickly going to
become a bottleneck, and we can't
iterate fast enough.
So, we need to invest into creating
offline or automatic evaluations. And
the key idea here is that instead of
verifying the solution quality with a
human, we need to find some sort of
automatic proxy for this, which in this
case is usually going to be some LM
judge or rubric.
And we won't talk deeply about the
differences between LM judges and
rubrics in this talk, but at a high
level, basically LM judges tend to be
given high-level quality guidelines, and
it's very similar to how humans evaluate
tasks. We give them our quality
guidelines, and they're going to
evaluate whether the solution adheres to
that. And it's the same set of quality
guidelines that we look at across all
different tasks that we're trying to
evaluate.
Rubrics, on the other hand, are a little
bit more specific. So, they define a
task-specific checklist of individual
items that are each separately verified
with
with an LM judge. So, one example of
this from the Dr. Tulu paper up here,
I like this example cuz it's both super
subjective, and it's also talking about
trying to culturally adapt a book into a
next Netflix film. But if we look at all
the rubric checks that the model is
looking at here, we're not looking at
some high-level like quality guideline.
We're outlining a checklist of specific
things that the LM judge needs to verify
within the solution that it's looking
at. So, it's task-specific, and we're
looking and verifying each of them
independently to make the evaluation way
more objective.
And what we end up with here is
automatic automatic metrics that we can
use to verify solution for quality in a
similar way to how a human would
evaluate a solution.
But the problem with this is that these
are all automatic metrics. They're just
a proxy, so they're going to be
imperfect. So, to solve this, we need to
do some sort of meta-evaluation to
ensure that our judge is accurate. And
what this means is that we'll take data
from the human evaluation process,
golden data. These are going to be
evaluation examples from humans that
we're confident in their quality. We
know these are good evaluation examples.
And then we want to measure the
agreement between what our judge or
rubric is telling us and this golden
data set. So, we basically just want to
look at basic things like correlation
metrics, binary accuracy, and so forth.
But meta-evaluation is like a pretty
wide space and there's a bunch of
different ways that you could approach
this. One example that I like to pull on
from Netflix, a project that I worked
on, we actually took an LLM judge and
showed that the outputs of this LLM
judge were causally correlated with key
streaming metrics like abandonment. So,
if your LLM judge tells you something is
bad, it's likely that somebody will
abandon the show after trying to watch
it. So, there's a bunch of different
possibilities for how to evaluate judges
and I'd encourage you to look into this
blog if you're interested in them.
And then finally, before moving on from
from meta-evaluation, one common
question is how to figure out what
agreement level is good. And for this,
it depends a lot on the task. Like more
subjective tasks, the level of agreement
that you can achieve is going to be a
lot lower. But what we can do is just
use human evaluation as a baseline. So,
we can look at the amount of agreement
between different humans who are trying
to evaluate this task, and we can shoot
for a similar level of agreement of our
judge with the humans. So,
similar levels of agreement both between
judges and humans and mutually between
humans.
And then from there, we have automatic
verifiers that we know work well. So, we
can just start to create benchmark
benchmarks around all of these
verifiers. To do this, it's pretty
similar to human evaluation. We just
sample data properly using the same
techniques we just talked about, and
then we use LLM judges or rubrics to
verify these outputs and then just try
and continually revise and improve the
data that we're evaluating on over time.
The only point that we still need to
talk about is that we now have multiple
non-deterministic components that we're
working with. In human evaluate
evaluations, we only had a
non-deterministic LLM. Now we have a
non-deterministic model and a
non-deterministic evaluator. So, we have
a lot of noise that we need to figure
out how to handle.
And in order to do this, we can just
apply the kitchen sink of different like
statistical methods to try and put
confidence intervals on all of this. So,
similarly to human evaluation, we can
use power analysis to tell us what the
size of our benchmark should be. We can
report error bars along with all of our
evaluation results and then use
techniques like resampling, which
basically just means taking multiple
rollouts from your LLM or from the
judges well to reduce variance.
And what we end up with is we don't just
report evaluation results. We report our
evaluation results with clear confidence
signals and then we take interventions
to try and make all of these confidence
signals as tight as possible. And if we
report those together, we can basically
more meaningfully detect capability
improvements in our model. We know if
one score on an eval is better, it's
because the model is actually better,
not because of noise or something like
this.
So now we have a calibrated human
evaluation process.
We've created offline evaluations and
calibrated judges that we can use to run
this automatically. So we can just run
this a bunch of different times and test
out tons of different ideas to scale the
experimentation process.
And then from there, we can take
whatever is working well and pass it
back to human evaluation to have humans
evaluate whether this is actually going
well.
And at this point, we might be asking
ourselves whether we're ready to deploy
this model or not.
And the answer could be yes, but if we
if we say yes at this point, we'd
actually be skipping a super important
part of the evaluation process, which is
production monitoring.
And the idea here is that we can define
and track production metrics for our
agent. So we're using how the agent is
used in production as another mechanism
for evaluating whether it's working
properly or not.
And to do this, you can look at a
variety of different metrics. Some of
them are explicit like thumbs up, thumbs
down feedback, preference feedback and
so forth. You'll see this done in like
chatbots all the time. But it could also
be implicit metrics like the length of a
session, abandonment rate and so on. So
you can define these different metrics
that are some somehow correlated to
whether the agent is performing well or
not.
And these are basically just quality
signals from production that we could
use to see if our agent is doing good.
And what we could do is we can take
these production metrics and measure
them in an AB test to get gain a
relative sense of how our agent is
doing. So, seeing compared to what we
already have in place, is the current
agent doing better than that? And again,
we can use a lot of statistical
techniques to tell us how long we need
to run this AB test and so forth. This
is related to power analysis, which we
talked about before.
And the nice thing about AB testing is
that what we could use what we could do
is basically treat this as a soft model
deployment process. So, instead of just
sending the model out to everybody, we
can vet the quality of this model in
production with an AB test and make sure
everything's going well before pursuing
a full rollout.
And even after we roll out the model,
there's a lot of opportunities to just
continually production monitor. We can
look for any concerning trends in
performance or even find cases where the
agent is failing, new use cases and so
forth, and use production to ground the
other evaluation steps in the real
world. So, production monitoring is
incredibly useful for extending evals,
finding new failure cases, all of these
things. We want to find all of these
cases and then pass them back to the
other parts of the evaluation process.
So, in this way, we just have to
continually work towards improving all
of the evaluation components over time.
Uh we've seen all of the different
components that we're going to cover in
this talk, uh but we can always make all
of them better. So, we could define new
or better quality criteria, we can
improve calibration of humans or judges,
or we could look at production to find
new error examples that we can work into
offline evals and so forth.
Or we could just take this entire
process and repeat it in a new new
domain. So, just build an entirely
different eval.
So,
to sum everything up, evaluation is
difficult, but for subjective tasks,
it's especially difficult because we're
dealing with more sources of noise. And
we've seen a roadmap and all of these
different components and tricks that we
can use to reduce the amount of noise as
much as possible to draw more confident
conclusions.
And in this roadmap, human evaluation
serves as our North Star for quality. It
provides a clear quality definition that
humans agree on. And then from this, we
could use this definition to calibrate
LLM judges or rubrics as a proxy to
human evaluation, and this allows us to
ex-scale the experimentation process.
Then anything that goes well, we can
pass it to human evaluation and
eventually deploy it. And when we
deploy, we can use AB testing,
production monitoring is another
evaluation mechanism to make sure
everything's going well in the real
world.
And this basically is something where we
have to fight noise at every step. So
because we're working with subjective
evaluations, we know that they're going
to be noisy. We need to be very
skeptical of evaluation results and try
and use statistics to give us like the
best picture of how our engine is
performing. So we can use techniques
like power analysis, confidence
intervals, resampling and more to reduce
the variance of the evaluation process
as much as possible and provide clearer
confidence signals.
And if we put all of this together, we
basically just end up with a multi-step
evaluation process. We run tons of
offline evals to give us an idea of
what's going to go well. We pass the
best ones to human evaluation to give us
a higher fidelity view of how something
is doing. And then we AB test it to kind
of test the waters in terms of well
whether it's doing well in production
and eventually deploy it. And once we
deploy, we can continue to monitor for
failure cases that we then work back
into all of the other steps of the
process.
All right. So I know that's a lot of
information, but for any areas that were
confusing or you want to read more
deeply into, I created this index here.
So this links out to further reading on
pretty much everything that we talked
about both from myself and other people.
So I encourage you to look into all of
these details if it's interesting to
you.
Thank you so much and I hope it was
helpful.
